title: Beyond Super-resolution: Unlocking the Potential of Fluorescence Microscopy at Its Resolution Limits and Quantitively Capability
content: Super-resolution microscopy has become an indispensable tool in cell biology, offering unprecedented insights into biological architectures with nanometer-level precision. This technology provides numerous advantages, including the ability to label multiple biomolecular targets with high specificity and simplified sample preparation. However, the high cost of super-resolution microscopes limits their widespread accessibility. To address this challenge, recent advancements have led to the development of more cost-effective super-resolution techniques, such as expansion microscopy (ExM) [1,2]. ExM achieves super-resolution through a unique approach, in which biological samples are embedded into expandable hydrogels. Upon exposure to an osmotic process, the specimen-hydrogel complex undergoes uniform expansion, effectively enhancing resolution in proportion to the expansion factor. Recently, we have developed innovative 4-fold and 12-fold isotropic 3D-Expansion Microscopy (4× and 12×3D-ExM) [3,4]. These methods enable a streamlined, single-step process for achieving robust and reproducible 3D isotropic expansion, applicable to both 2D and 3D cell culture models. With standard confocal microscopy, 12×3D-ExM achieves a lateral resolution of ∼15 nm and an axial resolution of ∼40 nm, allowing the visualization of nanoscale structures such as chromosomes, kinetochores, nuclear pore complexes, and Epstein–Barr virus particles. These results highlight the critical role of super-resolution microscopy in advancing our understanding of fundamental biological mechanisms.
